utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Gasi, may I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've made yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you may continue the examination-in-chief

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There's one matter that I wanted to bring to your attention, and I think it's fine to raise it in the presence of the witness. Regarding the Rule 70 materials for which we had not yet received permission yesterday, half an hour ago I received a call from the provider, advising me that written authorisation had been granted and he told me it was all right for me to disclose those materials. I have handed those to Defence counsel just before we started now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since this is a rather late disclosure, Mr. Stewart, I take it that I'll hear from the Defence if the time for preparing was too short.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I was just going to have a glance at it of course while we're in Court and let Your Honour know if there's any time we need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, I wanted to ask you about an incident at Luka camp where you were taken out to do some cleaning in Brcko town. Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not just any building. It was the SUP building in Brcko, the police station building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would you tell the Judges what happened on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in Luka, they picked out some 15 of us to work. They put us in a vehicle and they took us to the police station. The three of us were given the last floor to clean -- actually, an office, in which the windows were shattered. We were cleaning, and at one moment we heard noise in front of the building. I looked through the window, and on the other side where the SUP had its garages and restaurant in an open area, one of the police officers shot a civilian in the chest. Another civilian managed to escape and started running towards the exit. He may have made some ten metres, and then another policeman shot at him. He shot him in his legs. The man fell down and the guy who shot him in the first place approached him and shot him in the head. Some five or ten minutes later, somebody started shouting and running up the stairs, shouting: "Where are the other Turks? I'm going to kill them all." In the meantime, a local Serb appeared. He worked at the SUP at the time. He pushed us into another office and locked us in. And after that, when the situation calmed down, this same man came, unlocked the office, took us out, and then the people who brought us to the SUP building took us back to the Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Who were the people who had taken you to the police station for this cleaning detail and then took you back to Luka after?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were people who often came there. Amongst them was Miso Cajevic and a couple other local Serbs from Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were they wearing uniforms or were they with any particular military or police unit?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cajevic wore a camouflage uniform, olive-drab uniform. I don't know what army he belonged to. I suppose he belonged to the JNA. I don't know what the name of the army was. Others were also wearing similar clothes. There were some wearing civilian clothes, some wore police uniforms. There were all sorts of uniforms, and they were looking for volunteers to do the cleaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall how many volunteers you were in total that were taken to the SUP that day?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there was between 15 and 20 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were all of the others detainees at Luka with you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those who left the Luka with me, they were. But when we arrived at the SUP building, there were other people there, civilians. I don't know why they were there, but in any event, there were some other people. I don't know where they had been brought from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did the same number return to Luka at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the people from the group I knew. When I returned, there were only three of us in the vehicle with the policeman who took us back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you know the policeman that you saw doing any of the shooting?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him. I was watching, and the only thing I saw was that he wore police uniform. And there was another man with him also wearing a police uniform, a blue police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that short sleeve or long sleeve, and camouflage or plain blue?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a plain blue uniform. Both of them had plain blue uniforms. One of them had a short-sleeved blouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you feel comfortable telling us the name of the policeman who hid you or locked you in the room?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His name is Kaurinovic. Boro is his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to ask you about the time that you were in Brcko between the blowing up of the bridge on 30 April and your release from Luka on 7 June. Can you tell the Court, as best you remember, all the different military, paramilitary, and police groups that you saw in Brcko or in Luka camp.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 12th of May onwards, when I was moving around, I had several opportunities to leave the Elektrodistribucija and go to the town in order to do repairs. In the town itself, there were several checkpoints, mixed checkpoints, manned by people in camouflage uniforms, for whom I suppose that they belonged to the JNA. And sometimes there would also be one or two police officers wearing regular police uniforms. It all depended on the checkpoint. If you were to go towards Grcica, where my father resides, by the Teslak [phoen] factory, that was the biggest checkpoint that I could notice at the time. This checkpoint was manned by the Red Berets, by people in camouflage uniforms, not only olive-drab camouflage uniforms, but also blue camouflage uniforms. And some of the local Serbs from Brcko, my neighbours, were stopping vehicles and asked for the people's IDs. In the Luka itself, in the hangar, I saw people from the Serbian MUP. On one occasion they came, they stopped a blue Golf in front of the vehicle, and on the door of that vehicle you could see the coat of arms of the Republic of Serbia and the inscription "the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia." The three men in the vehicle, they escorted Kosta into the hangar. They wanted to see some Muslim sniper shooters. Those were two people that I knew from Brcko. They were very close to me in the hangar. And one of them wore a camouflage uniform and insignia of a JNA major, and the other two who accompanied them, they had coat of arms of Serbia on their sleeves and one of them had the coat of arms of the former Yugoslavia, which means that one of them was from the federal SUP and one from the republican SUP. They told me: "Kosta, where are those Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Muslim sniper shooters?" They approached Muhamed, also known as Jovo, who is still alive to this day, luckily enough. And they asked him: "Why are you here?" The major asked him that. And the poor man, he didn't -- could not even use the proper word. He said that he was a sniper shooter. The major then swore and said: "If all the Muslim sniper shooters are like this one here, I would not have lost any men. Why don't you, Kosta, look after this man, provide him with some medical help?" On that same day or the day after a local doctor appeared and he helped these two men. And later on, they allowed us to be brought fresh water into the hangar, so that people could have a drink of fresh water. Yesterday, I described a situation when five or six men stormed into the hangar. They forced us to sing Serbian songs. They all wore camouflage uniforms. It was dark, but I could still see them. They spoke in a Serbian accent. They forced us to sing Serbian songs. I did not see any of their insignia. Ivan, who beat me up on the first day, he bore the insignia of an Arkan's Tiger. The guy who took me out from the Luka, he wore a camouflage uniform, a red beret, a military police belt. On one of his shoulders -- on one occasion, Vojvoda Mirko Blagojevic came with his escorts. We all knew him. We all greeted him in the Serbian way. They wore camouflage uniforms. They introduced themselves as Serbian Chetniks, Radicals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a minute. Do you know where Mirko Blagojevic was from?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know who the leader of the Serb Radical Party was at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? In Bijeljina or --? At the federal level?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Blagojevic was in Bijeljina, and at the federal level, in Belgrade, it was Vojvoda Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned a man named Ivan who had the insignia of Arkan's unit. Can you tell us what that insignia looked like?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On his sleeve, either on his left or the right sleeve, I could see Arkan's Tiger, the head of an Arkan's Tiger. On the left-hand side of his chest, a small flag of the Republika Srpska. When he arrived in the hangar, he did not have a cap on his head. In any case, he wore a camouflage uniform, which is very interesting. His boots were different than the ones that I saw on JNA soldiers up to then. His boots were different. They differed. He also had a pistol and a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you also meet a man named Mauzer in Brcko during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer. I had an opportunity while I was in Elektro-Brcko to see him when he arrived with his assistants. They pulled their car and they asked our director to line us up. We were lined up. Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, came out, started asking what our names were. He separated the Serbs who worked with us to one side, and the Muslims and one Croat to another side. There were more Muslims than Serbs in Elektrodistribucija at that time. He started walking from one man to another. He asked what our names were. He started threatening us, blaming us for things. He said that one of his fighters died on an operating table because we Muslims, electricians, cut the power off so that he could not be operated on. I really didn't know what he was talking about. I was clueless. After some time, after having waved his pistol for a while -- they didn't hit us, but he swore at us and he also lectured our director. But then the situation calmed down. And after that, we almost became friends with the same people who shouted at us and who cursed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were they in civilian clothes or military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three of them wore uniforms. Interestingly enough, the two escorts wore complete uniforms, whereas he himself wore Adidas trainers on his feet. He did not have a helmet. He did not have a hat on his head. But he did have a uniform, and he also had a radio set. He had a radio set on his body.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were the men with him armed as well?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them had an automatic rifle, and the other one, I don't know. I only saw this rifle in American movies before the war. I really don't know where that rifle came from. It was a one-barreled rifle, and the other one had an automatic rifle. And Mauzer, he pulled out his pistol and waved his pistol at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know if he was a local from Brcko or did he come from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mauzer is not from Brcko. He's from Bijeljina as well. The other two also were not from Brcko. One of them introduced himself as Captain Dusko Tuzlandzic if my memory serves me well. He had long hair. That's interesting for a captain to have long hair. You don't see that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know if Mauzer's unit had a name or a nickname?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he is the commander of the Serbian Volunteer Guard. That's how he introduced himself before he started lecturing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to ask you about the day that you were released from Luka camp. I think you told us yesterday that was 7 June. Can you tell us how that happened?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 7th of June, maybe around 11.00, between 11.00 and 12.00. A car stopped in front of the hangar, a Pajero jeep. Five or ten minutes later, a man in a camouflage uniform entered the hangar, followed by Kosta. He stood in the middle of the hangar and called out my name, and he said: "Get up, Isak. On your feet. Come closer." I came closer to him. He gave me his hand. We shook hands, and he said: "I'm glad to see you. I have greetings to convey to you." I say: "Who from?" He said: "Your wife." And I say: "Did you see her personally?" And he said: "No. Some friends were with her and told me to convey her greetings to you personally in Luka." So I said: "Thank you very much." And then Kosta said something along the lines: "Don't be afraid. Be relaxed. We're friends. We're colleagues. Don't be afraid." In the hangar, this lasted for some five or ten minutes. All the people around us were listening to this exchange, and then Kosta says: "Captain, we could have gone to my office. Maybe both you and Isak could have a cup of coffee there. Maybe you could get acquainted better." And then this other guy said: "Yes. That's a good idea. Why don't we go to your office and have a cup of coffee." I went out of the hangar. We were sitting in Kosta's office. Kosta put the kettle on for a cup of coffee. Some guards were entering the office and looking at this soldier, this special. We were talking about sports. He asked me if I knew some people in Belgrade. I said I knew some athletes, like myself. The kettle took a long time to boil. And then I said: "Captain, I'm really not keen on coffee. Why don't you let me go back to the hangar?" And he says: "You're a good man. Maybe there will be another opportunity for us to have a cup of coffee together, and now you may go." As I was leaving the office, he called me again and said: "Man, what can I do for you?" He says: "You're a good man." I say: "Nothing. You just let me go, if you're a friend, if you're a colleague." And he says: "I'll do my utmost to help you." And then I said: "Am I free?" He says: "Yes, you are. Go back to the hangar." I went back to the hangar, and then through the door of the hangar, I saw the vehicle leaving on that same day after 2.00 or 3.00, again the same car re-appeared. Then this captain and another Red Beret soldier, known as Dugi, or Pedja, and Rade, my friend, came. Kosta was with them, of course. Kosta was carrying my ID and a piece of paper, and he said: "Isak, the time has come for you to start rowing again for Yugoslavia. You are going home. You're free to go." I said goodbye to all the other people in the hangar, and that's how it was. This man put me in that car.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Did he -- had he introduced himself to you yet? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He introduced himself as Rade Bozic, the moment he came to that hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you said he had a camouflage uniform. Did he have -- was he wearing any insignia or any rank on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He wore the insignia. When the JNA people wear camouflage uniforms, the insignia usually is here in the front, and his were those of a captain. And also, he had a white belt. This white belt which he wore with the buckle is the type of belt that the military police wore in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was he wearing or carrying any type of helmet or hat?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't wear a cap on his head, but he had it on one of his shoulders. It was folded and placed on his shoulder. It was a red beret.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the men with him, were they dressed the same way or differently?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second time when he appeared in the hangar, this Pedja Dugi was with him, and he wore the same uniform, he had the same pistol, and he even had a radio with him, on him, and he also had a red beret on his head. Kosta was wearing the clothing that he usually wore. He had the blue shirt, the blue pants, of the police uniform, and also a police cap on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe that you have told us before that you were first taken home to get some things, and where did you go immediately after that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I took my things, he told me: Now you're going on a longer trip. He didn't tell me where I was going. Then we went past the Elektrodistribucija. We came out there for a couple of minutes. And those people there saw me together with them. Then we started driving towards Bijeljina. Before we went to Brcko, there is a gas station, and we turned right. We went to the customs area. So in front of the customs area we stopped. There is a little guardhouse and a fence, and there were people sitting in front of it. There's a large parking place in front of the customs building. There were many vehicles there from the JNA, the Serbian MUP. On the wall they had written out which unit and to which part of the military the parking was allocated to. There was also even space for the special units of the Serbian ministry, also for Radicals and Chetniks from Serbia there was space. There were vehicles there. Amongst them was a blue-painted pinzgauer, a camouflage-painted one. There was a whole line of vehicles there. I also saw a couple of people dressed in the same way as Rade was. They wore these camouflage uniforms, the multicoloured uniforms. Some of them had caps on their heads, some were not wearing them but had them folded on their shoulders. Later when we set off for Bijeljina, Rade said that at that place in the customs area, people from Serbia, Specials, were sleeping there, members of the Serbian MUP, of the military, also the Radicals, Seselj's soldiers, Arkan's men. He said mostly all the people from Serbia proper were sleeping there, that there were no locals there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did Rade Bozic do while you were at that location?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He left the car. He went outside, out of the car and left me inside the car. There is a guardhouse at the front, like a reception area, and he went inside that little building. And I saw him talking to the person on duty there, who passed him a telephone receiver. And then Rade came back and said: "Well, it seems that I have to stay here." There was some reason, but he didn't say what it was. And while he was talking to me, the man from the office start to wave back at me and then he ran off back there and then again he spoke to somebody on the telephone. I saw that through the window. And then he came back and he made this sign and said: "Yes. Everything will be okay." And that's when he told me: "We're going to Belgrade. That's where your wife is. So I'm taking you there now." Then we started to drive towards Bijeljina, and later we went to Ugljevik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did you eventually go to that day?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ended up in Zvornik. And on the way from Ugljevik to Zvornik, he told me: "Do you know, my man, who is releasing you from Luka?" I said I don't know. I really didn't know; I had no idea at the time. He said: "Captain Dragan. Do you know who that is?" And I said: "Yes, I do," because I read something about that in the papers. I don't know when the war was going on in Croatia. I read about his Red Berets. And he said: "Yes. He, personally, the big boss himself, was the one who issued the order for you to be released." And he said: "He will personally wait for you in Zvornik. He wants to meet you. He has heard many good things about you," he said. I said: "All right. Very well." So we were just -- continued to drive, and during the drive there was talk. And on one occasion, Rade Bozic - and I didn't ask him anything - he told me himself: "I'm going to tell you a secret now that many Serbs don't know of. I was the one who commanded the operation to blow up the bridges over the Sava River." And that he was very sorry that many civilians were casualties in that operation. That's what he said. But there you are. It was war. I guess they didn't really programme the action very well. He said the Croats had released the civilians before they were supposed to do that, and we, he said, had to blow up the bridge, and that's how it happened. And I don't know. We talked about some other things. I didn't ask him anything. I was just surprised why he was telling me all of these things. But yes, he told them to me. So we came to Zvornik. There is a motel there. He parked in front of the motel. The street lights were beginning to come on and I could see people sitting in front. They were all in camouflage uniforms. They were mixed up. There were Red Berets, Arkan's soldiers there. And I could see that everybody knew him there because when he parked the car, they were asking him who is this man and he said: "He's ours." And when he was leaving the car, Captain Dragan appeared in civilian clothes and another journalist, a journalist from Ilustrovana Politika was with him, and there was another woman there as well. Later she introduced herself as his secretary from the fund. He extended his hand. He said: "Where are you, Isak? How are you?" As if we knew each other. "You're a good man."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you ever met him before?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I did not meet him before. I didn't have the opportunity to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you seen him before?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him once in Brcko. I think it was him. He was together with the local Serbs. And of course I saw him on television. On those occasions, he was also in civilian clothes. This was before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during your ride to Zvornik from Brcko, did Rade Bozic tell you what unit he was a part of?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did. I asked him, and he said he was a professional captain in the JNA, in the Special Units of the military police, for special operations. We were talking about this when we left Brcko. I mean, the man kept talking. I don't know. I didn't ask him very much, but he kept talking by himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you find out how he happened to come to Luka in the first place and arrange for your release? How did he know about you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you before that the big boss, aka Captain Dragan, ordered for me to be released from there. Later, when it was all over, when I had already met Captain Dragan and the people from his fund, and later I found out from my wife and from a friend, a sports friend of mine who had intervened on my behalf with Captain Dragan, that I would -- so that I would be released from Luka. And all of that was initiated thanks to the Serbian lieutenant whom I had met in Luka and to whom I had given the phone number where my wife was. So later when they found out from this man where I was, they then saw where they could go to ask for my release. My wife staged a scene in front of Captain Dragan. I don't know. I guess he liked her. He liked the way she was conducting herself. So he promised her that the next day, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or within 48 hours, as he said. She didn't believe him, and he said: "Well, you can be sure I'm going to bring him to you to Belgrade." So that's how it was. Anyway, that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after you met Captain Dragan in Zvornik, where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He sat down, and that woman, that secretary from the fund, and that journalist, they all sat in the same car. So we crossed the Drina from Bosnia and entered Serbia. There is a road there. The Serbians built it. And when they saw him, they didn't even ask to see our IDs. They wanted to have a photo taken together with him. "Oh, Captain Dragan, how are you?" All the Serbians knew about him. "How is it going in Bosnia?" And he said: "The next time I stop by I will have a picture taken with you." So then we just passed by, and during our drive we stopped for a break, a little bit before Loznica. And then he came to the back seat where I was sitting. And then he started to tell me: "Well, you saw where you were over there in Luka." He said: "A human head is not worth the -- a head of cabbage there. Be very careful what you say. Be very careful what you do. You are a good man. Your wife is first-class and I will deliver you to her. Don't worry. But I do have one request to make of you." And I asked him: "What is it?" And he said: "When you come to Belgrade, I will give you two or three days. Sit down, recover a little bit, take a piece of paper or two, and write down for me what you saw in Brcko from perhaps the 30th of April until you were there until the 7th of July. Who took you to Luka, why they took you, what date were you taken to Luka, where did you move around town, how did you move around, why were you moving around. So just do that for me. You don't have to write more than two pages. You can write that in your own handwriting. And I will read it. And that is all that I am asking you to do. Just come to the fund premises, tell the people at the reception that you need to see me. They will allow you to do that. They will be expecting you. They'll know you'll be coming to see me." So I did that. I wrote it all down. And then two or three days later I did go to the fund premises and I gave it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened to those pages that you gave him that you had written?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his office, there was this friend of mine, this sports friend of mine. He drove me there. I didn't have a car at the time. We sat down. I gave him the paper. He read it through and he told me: "Yes, you did a good job." And then he said: "I have to give this to some woman over there for her to type out, so it's more legible, and when it's all finished, you'll see I'll take the paper that you wrote and I will tear it up." So we were just sitting there in the office, and then in about five or ten minutes this woman typed it all out and she brought the typed sheets back to him, and the sheets that I had written by hand, he took and he tore them up. The sheets that she had typed up, he took. Then he called somebody on the phone and he said: "Can you hear me? This is Marti here." And he said: "I'm just going to send you something through the fax." And he faxed the pages. And I guess the person on the other side of the line said: "Well, give me a few minutes. I just want to read what is here first and then I'll get back to you." And we sat there for 15 minutes. We were talking about different things, sports and so on. And then he called back that same person again and he said: "What do you think about this report that's written?" I guess he meant my report. I don't know. And then he turned around again to me and he said: "Everything is all right." Like he was giving me a green light or something. He said: "You've done your job. Now you are free and if you ever need any help to get a personal ID card or a refugee card in Belgrade, just come here and I will take care of all of that for you. Just ask to see me and they will let you through here." Then I left the fund offices and I went back to my friend's again. I went twice. I tried on two occasions, because both of my brothers, and one of my brother's sons, they were in Luka. Then all three of them later were at Batkovic. I met him again on one occasion, and I asked him whether he could help me, and he said: "Well, I'll see what I can do." And then I heard nothing from him and I went to see him again, and he said: "Don't come and see me here any more. If I can do anything, I will call you at your friend's house and then you will hear from me." Since that time, I never heard from him again. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the pages that you wrote up for him about what had happened in Brcko. What did you write down about what happened in Brcko? Did you write about the killings that you had seen?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't write about the killings. I didn't write about -- all that I wrote was that on the 27th of May, 1992, two Serbian police officers from Brcko came and arrested me, took me to the SUP, took me to Luka, beat me up. I was beaten up by a man called Ivan, dressed in such-and-such a uniform. I didn't talk about the Red Berets. I didn't talk about the people who came to the hangar. I didn't talk about Ranko Cesic and that incident. I didn't talk about the pile of dead bodies behind the hangar towards the Sava. I didn't talk about the murder of two people in the police station. I didn't talk about the things that I heard from the inmates at Luka. Perhaps I lied to him on purpose. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. Perhaps if you were in my position, maybe you would do the same thing. I wanted to save my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you think he didn't really want to hear about what had happened in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know why he asked me for that report. If he wanted a realistic report, he had his own men there, so he could have gotten a proper report. If they were honourable men, they probably did send reports about what those same Red Berets and Arkan's soldiers did in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, I'd like to show the witness the next exhibit in our sequence. Yes. 39.022? I'm sorry. This is the new one. This is the map. What number would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P21.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, can you see that on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, but it's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would it be easier if you had a hard copy to look at?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May we hand the witness a hard copy? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us what that piece of paper is?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the paper that I brought to the courtroom yesterday. That's the map of the town of Brcko, with the markings. If you wish, I can go through it and explain what I marked with 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. If you would, could you begin with number 1 and tell us what location is marked by number 1, number 2, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1 is one of the bridges. That's the bridge that's used only for passenger traffic. When it was working, also cars could pass over it. Number 2 is the SUP building. Number 3 is the Luka and the hangars. Number 4 is the building of the JNA, the barracks. Number 4 [sic] is about more or less the corner where my building, my apartment building, is located, where I used to live, on the third floor, like I said yesterday. Number 5 is the Elektrodistribucija, where I worked until the 9th or 10th of May, when I was taken to Luka. Number 6 is the power transmission line that passes through the firing range and that place that we talked about yesterday. Number 8 is -- 6 is that place where the photograph with the mass grave was taken. Number 7 is the place where, on one occasion, I drew the location where I saw that same TAM truck and the bulldozer which was burying those bodies that they were unloading from the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. TAM truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about number 1. That's the bridge that we saw a picture of earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the apartment where you lived is marked here with the number 4, and then "APT" written under it?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's it. The barracks is the -- this compound of buildings here, that's number 4. And here I just wrote where my apartment was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You can set that aside for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could we show another exhibit to the witness? It would be our number 49.03. It's the summary of the events in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P22.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, if you could look at the cover sheet of the B/C/S version of that document. Can you read us the title of that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Summary of the events and situations with an assessment of the degree of achievement." Is that what you're thinking of?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. That's it. Have you seen this document before today?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that here in this building when you were preparing to testify?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You gave it to me to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you ever seen it before that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you able to read the signature on the last page of that document?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told you what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would you tell the Judges what you think that signature is.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djordje Ristanic, the commander of the War Presidency at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not he held that position at that time in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know 100 per cent that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you know Djordje Ristanic before the war?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I knew him very well. We went to school together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to read that summary before coming to Court today?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And based on your experience during the time you were in Brcko in April and May of 1992, to the extent that that describes those events, is it consistent with what you saw and experienced?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is written down here, more or less, is actually what happened. In some places, he mixes up the people from the paramilitary groups, and he mixes up the JNA garrison where they actually received the weapons from and from where everything was coordinated. And even in the report here he says that they did not have good cooperation with the garrison, which is a pure lie. That is my experience. And then he says paramilitary groups which looted. That is also a pure lie, as if they weren't able to prevent that. Actually, they coordinated everything with them here. This report is, I think, presenting a realistic situation in Brcko in 1992. Well, there are some places where he's fudging and says that the War Presidency leadership didn't know about certain things, that they couldn't be prevented, and so on. In my opinion, there was no uncontrolled chaos in Brcko, but everything was controlled and coordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You can set that aside for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next item I would like to show --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry. The next exhibit I would like to show the witness, I think we may be skipping one in what we've given to the registrar before. It would be our Exhibit 37.188, which is a video. I'm not intending to play the video at this time, Your Honour. It's about an hour long. But I have the transcript of the video. I would like to show the transcript to the witness and ask him some questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first ask the registrar, and you, Mr. Hannis: We have been provided with a translation as well. Would that have the same exhibit number or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P22.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have been provided not only with a B/C/S version, but also with an exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which is in English. From what I understood from the witness is the translation, because the title was translated in a similar way as what I find on the top of the other document. And was that part of the exhibit or is that a separate exhibit? Because -- or am I mistaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is ERN 00967572 on the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be an exhibit, and from the numbering from the registrar, I understood that it gets the same number but with dot 1 added.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. And then I wanted to talk about the video, but we want to present to the witness the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I then take it that you only tender the transcript and not the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I consult? Excuse me a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was my intention first of all to ask him about what's in the transcript. He has watched the video and he's read the transcript. We also have four still photos that have been made of individuals appearing in the video that I propose to show him. But it was not my intention to play the video at this time. But we did want to tender the video and perhaps play it later with another witness or offer it later on. It has not been synchronised yet, so for purposes of trying to show an English translation as a B/C/S video is playing, it's not an appropriate time for us to try to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So for the moment, you only tender what you say is the transcript of the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Although I intended to ask him if he had actually seen the video on which this transcript is based.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The transcript will be Prosecution Exhibit number P23, and the translation in English, P23.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, can you read the top line of that document you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The report: "It was the last day of April, 1992. Several hundreds of people gathered on the left bank, the Croatian side."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is there is a title on the top line?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It just says "Exhibit transcript," no title.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Gasi. I'm looking at the English, which has a title, and I see that the B/C/S does not. Let me ask you: Have you seen this document before testifying this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You gave it to me to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you read the whole thing before today?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You asked me to do that, and I read all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, may I just interrupt you? You say that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the English version has a title on top of it and the B/C/S version not. I have some difficulties in identifying any difference as far as titles are concerned, apart from difference -- letter A and letter B after the OTP reference number. But I do not see any title.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Looking at my notes, I see what I was looking at was a cover page that was just separately attached to my English translation that says "Documentary film, the Brcko file."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you also watch the video on which this transcript is taken from?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There are a number of people that appear in that video. Did you know most or all of those people that appear in the film?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know all the people on this video footage, all but one person at the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which person was that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Secretary of State of the United States of America, Mrs. Madeleine Albright.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And based on your experiences during your time in Brcko in April and May of 1992 and your knowledge of the persons appearing in this video, is the information contained therein accurate and consistent with what you saw and heard?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have told you here, what I went through and what people are saying in this video is all the same thing. It's the truth of the events that took place in Brcko at the time. Some of the people that appear in this video footage were with me in the Luka during the same time, and I'm very glad to see that they have survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, Your Honour, we have taken four separate video stills from the video, and I would like to show those to the witness one at a time. I don't know if it is easier to number this as one item, and we'll have them shown to him one after another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. May I take it, since the video has not been shown to the Chamber, that Defence has had an opportunity to see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To be frank, Your Honour, I'm not sure whether we've even had an opportunity, but if we've had an opportunity, bluntly, it's not one that we've realised we had. We're not aware that we've got this video, but maybe we have. Have we?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I said I'd be frank about it. I think we have got it, but we haven't watched it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do understand that at a later stage it will be shown anyhow, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that it will be shown anyhow at a later stage of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's our intention, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, can you see that photo on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it, no. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see four individuals pictured there. Can you start from the left-hand corner, then go left, right, then down, and tell us who each of those four individuals are, if you know.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Top left corner, Arkan. Top right corner, Vojislav Seselj. Bottom left corner, Mirko Jovic. Bottom right corner, the person who took me out of the Luka camp, Captain Dragan. It was on his orders that I was taken out of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And of those four, I think the only one you haven't talked about before is Mirko Jovic. Can you tell us who he was and whether he was in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was in Brcko, but his soldiers did make an appearance in the Luka on several occasions. They were White Eagles. Whether he was in Luka personally or not, I don't know, but his soldiers did come to the Luka camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what kind of uniform or insignia did they have that distinguished them from other groups?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only difference was that they had white eagles on their arms, and they introduced themselves as White Eagles. There are just slight differences between their uniforms and the uniforms of those soldiers belonging to Rade Bozic. The uniforms that Arkan's soldiers had and Dragan's soldiers had were somewhat darker, whereas White Eagles's uniforms were a bit lighter. They were still camouflage uniforms. That was the only difference that I could notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May we show him the next still photo in the sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise the gentleman in that picture, sir?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Beli Vojinovic, the president of the Brcko SDS at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us who that is, please.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And finally, the fourth one. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djordje Ristanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, Mr. Gasi, I have one more exhibit I want to ask you about. Before we move on to that, may I ask what number we gave those sequence of photos?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The set of four photographs will be Prosecution Exhibit number P24.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next one is an autopsy report. I only want to show the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Prosecution. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I only want to show the witness page 7 of that particular document. I believe it's 00636317.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. That's in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Correct. Thank you. I think that's sufficient for our purposes. No. We'll have him look at both. And for the record, Your Honour, this is a page from one of the expert reports that we filed in this case of autopsies that were taken from bodies recovered in the Brcko area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, at the top of that page you'll see a list of five names from the autopsy report done by Dr. Hunt, an expert witness listed in this case. Do you recognise any of those five names as people that you knew in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sakib Becirovic, Franjo Vugrincic and the guy at the top, Almir Tursic. But I know Sakib Becirovic and Franjo Vugrincic personally. I believe that I know the others as well. I believe that all of them are from Brcko, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were any of these people in Luka at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear from the other prisoners at Luka about what had happened to Mr. Becirovic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard from a man who was a member of the Partizan club. He said that Sakib Becirovic, also known as Kibe, had been killed in front of the Partizan stadium and that it was Ranko Cesic who killed him. This man also told me that on that same day Ranko Cesic killed four or five other men in addition to Kibe. This man mentioned all of their names. He knew exactly who they were. I didn't recognise any of those names. In any case, he told me that Kibe was killed on that same day in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Your Honour, for the record, you may recall Mr. Cesic pled guilty to the murder of Mr. Becirovic. I have no further questions for Mr. Gasi at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, one question: Will you tender only page 7 of the report or the whole of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I consult with Mr. Harmon for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's our intention to eventually file the whole report. The status of our experts on autopsies was still somewhat up in the air. We had been trying to reach an agreement with the prior Defence counsel but had not arrived at that point. I think we currently listed Dr. Hunt as a 92 bis (D) witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I couldn't confirm that, as a matter of fact, by heart. But would it not be wise if no other questions have been put to the witness, apart from whether he knew the five individuals named at page 7, to at this moment to limit ourselves to page 7? Because otherwise all the rest would be in evidence as well, which might not be the appropriate way of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Page 7, bearing the ERN number 00636317 would then be Exhibit number --?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Since nothing of the text has been discussed in whatever way, I think it's just a matter of recognition of five names. So therefore, perhaps the translation in English is even not needed, and perhaps it's even better that we do not have any knowledge apart from that there are appearing five names -- this is the English version, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The page number I have referred to was the English version, yes, Your Honour, but I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. Yes. So this concluded your examination-in-chief, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, all parties in a trial have the right to examine you. You'll now be examined by counsel for the Defence. Is it you, Mr. Stewart, or is it Ms. Loukas who is going to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's me, Your Honour. But I wonder, in light of the fact that we were handed that statement at the beginning of the afternoon, and the fact that we have been running for an hour and a quarter, I'm, of course, in the Tribunal's hands but I wonder whether the convenient thing would be simply to take the break that would be due in 15 minutes at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would not mind, I'd rather continue, because I have to take into consideration the length of the tapes, and we get in trouble later on --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we have then a longer session later on. So if it would be possible for you to start the cross-examination and then we would have a break in some 12 to 13 minutes. It's both a question of interpreters spreading more or less the time available, and also a matter of tape length. So if that would be possible for you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think that's going to be a problem, Your Honour. Well, if after 10 minutes or so I've got to that point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- We'll see how we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, could I just take my wig off? Because it's a lot easier. I hope Your Honour doesn't mind me being half-dressed in the national style, but it's a bit ridiculous with the headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From my past, I remember that some of your learned friends would consistently refuse to take their wigs off ever when in court, but I leave it entirely up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I clearly haven't refused, Your Honour, and neither has Your Honour refused me the privilege.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, just a couple of I hope not at all difficult points to start with. Yesterday, when you were asked the day when you had left Luka, you gave an answer, 7th of July exactly. That was at page 64 of yesterday's transcript. And today, at one point, about three minutes to 3.00, you said the same thing again. You referred to the 7th of July. But I believe it's quite clear from the rest of your evidence that your consistent position is it is the 7th of June that you left.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. How could you hear me talking about the 7th of July? Because I know it was on the 7th of June, 1992, and I said that yesterday, and I have repeated it today. So how could you hear me saying 7th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, we don't need to fall out over this at all. You have given me exactly the confirmation that I was asking for. It's only through a slip of the tongue, no doubt, on the transcript the 7th of July appears. So that's simply cleared up for everybody's benefit. We're not in disagreement at all about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just -- I'd like to explain to Mr. Gasi. Mr. Gasi, your original B/C/S, that is, Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian words, are translated into English. I do not know. Sometimes there is just a translation that might not to the full extent be correct. So what you said yesterday, we always can check it if we want to, but it could well be that it appears for us as July, where you say you said June. This is not something to bother about, and the matter has been clarified. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're looking puzzled, Mr. Gasi. I want to make it very clear that on this particular point you're not under any attack, there isn't any disagreement between us. Whatever disagreements we might reach on other matters. You're still looking puzzled, but, well, I'll proceed. The next point is this: That you have referred I think once or twice in your evidence to SMB camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, SMB, as I understand it, they're the words in your language, but SMB simply stands for the three words which are in English, and it will be translated for you, of course, grey-olive colour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Grey-olive colour, yes. Grey-olive colour. S is grey, M is olive, B is colour. So that's what the abbreviation stands for. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But isn't it correct that generally there are uniforms which are described as SMB, and there are uniforms that are described as camouflage uniforms, but in fact, they're two different styles of uniform?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. While I was serving in the army, there was just one shade of SMB, of olive colour, grey-olive colour, and it lasted for a while. However, they also had camouflage olive-grey uniforms, even when I was in the army. There were some special army branches that used to wear olive-drab camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, do you remember that you gave an interview way back in -- or you were interviewed way back in 1993, in Copenhagen, by a body called the Danish Helsinki Committee?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What were the circumstances in which you were interviewed? Let me ask you this: How did you come to be in Denmark?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a refugee there. I went to Macedonia first, then to Bulgaria, Romania, then Ukraine, all of Poland. Then from Poland, I took a ferry to Copenhagen. I went from Belgrade to Macedonia first, and then I did all this travelling that I've just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Well, then you arrived in Copenhagen when?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 16 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your interview, then, was in May 1993, the 7th of May, 1993 is the date. Does that figure for you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And we have prepared on the Defence side -- it's a clip or a small bundle of materials which I would like the witness, and of course everybody else, the Tribunal and everybody else, to have. They're indexed and numbered. And in particular, if you go to what's described on the index as 3-A, well, 3-B in your case, Mr. Gasi, at page 20 of the B/C/S version, and at page 11 is the English.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 11? Is it 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's 20, the B/C/S version, page 20. Page 11 is the English version.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I should say, Your Honour, just for the record, the numbering on the left-hand side, that's been added by me, because it just seemed to be very inconvenient if we were trying to look for paragraphs, especially since they don't completely tally as far as the page layout is concerned. So, for the record, that's been added on both versions, by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 2, could you just cast your eye down paragraph 2 and paragraph 3, and I think you can then confirm that those paragraphs aren't accurate in the sense that they're consistent with the evidence that you've so far given to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is disputable here? Is there something missing or did I omit something from my testimony that you can find here in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll tell you what we'll do, Mr. Gasi. We will -- it will all become clear, no doubt, but we'll continue with me asking the questions, Mr. Gasi, and if you would do your best to answer them. So my question is, if you cast your mind down paragraphs -- cast your eye down paragraphs 2 and 3, do you agree that's consistent with your current position and the evidence that you've given to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in Brcko. My father is Albanian, mother is a Muslim, I lived in Brcko, I was an athlete, a canoe rower, I was politically engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't necessarily invite you to read the whole thing out loud. I'm just asking if you've read to yourself the paragraphs and confirm what I've suggested which is that it's entirely consistent with your current position and the evidence that you've given to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second paragraph that you marked, 3, it says here -- maybe this is what you're looking for. A neighbour of mine took me --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... not to be looking all the time for what I'm looking for. Let me worry about that. If you could just please answer my questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could we give Mr. Gasi time to read so that he can confirm, because that's what he started doing aloud. But -- Mr. Gasi, you may read paragraphs 2 and 3 and then answer the question.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's okay. We can move on. I subscribe to everything that I read here. Is that your point? Was that the purpose of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 4, Mr. Gasi. In Brcko there was no resistance against the federal army, only some shooting at the barricades and the Muslim parts of the town. The Muslims had panicked and taken refuge in a Muslim part of the town, and - you're G, you're described as - who had confidence in the federal army, remained in your flat next to the barracks in the central part of the town. So it's correct that you had confidence in the federal army at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the next sentence: "The worst deeds were committed not by the army but by paramilitary groups which arrived after the army." And that's correct as well, is it?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we move on to a reference in this document, at paragraph 9, numbered paragraph 9, do you see that you refer to Pudic. Read that paragraph to yourself, please. It's quite a short paragraph. And just note the reference at the end to Pudic, Jovan, or perhaps it's Jovan Pudic.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw these photos in Belgrade, and which committee showed them to me in Helsinki, they showed me a copy from the British Guardian, depicting a policeman in a police uniform shooting in the back of some civilians. I didn't say that I knew that person in the photo. I told them that I saw this photographer in Belgrade, the photographer who had taken these photos in Brcko. And one of these photos depicts Jovan Pudic. I don't know how this came into the interview. I did not have an opportunity to correct anything in it. I returned to the centre where I lived, and later on I was provided with an English copy of this text, and that's where the mistake arises from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the -- let's see how far there was a mistake. Is the position simply that you were able, at least on one photograph, to identify Pudic Jovan, or Jovan Pudic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the building of the Helsinki Watch, when I was giving the interview, people showed me a copy of the photo from the Guardian, and I told them that I couldn't recognise the man in that particular photo, but I saw some other photos taken by the same photographer. I read this text. I did not say that the person depicted in the photo that they showed to me on that occasion was Jovan Pudic. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see it's just on a quarter to. I don't know whether that is now a convenient time for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's an appropriate time to have a break. Mr. Gasi, we'll have a break for 20 minutes. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, I'm going to have handed to you, and we also have copies for the Tribunal and everyone else, a statement, in your case, Mr. Gasi, in B/C/S, but otherwise available in English, a statement that you gave on the 4th, 5th, and 11th of April, 1995, being interviewed by Susan Castro and Frederick Buckley on behalf of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Does the witness have that now, the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Gasi, do you remember making this statement over a period of three days in April 1995?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether it was three days, but it was definitely two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It records three days on the front, so -- but I don't think that need be an issue between us, Mr. Gasi. If you go to page 5 of the statement, I hope there's a reasonable match in the page layout. Can you find a paragraph that begins: "On May 27th, 1992 ..." On the English version it's right in the middle of page 5. Can you find that, Mr. Gasi? It should be on page 5, or very close. It begins with the date. It says: "On May 27th".

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour and Mr. Stewart. I have a version in B/C/S with paragraphs numbered that may help him find his way more easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it might, yes. Thank you. I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a very helpful suggestion. The only thing is I don't have the key to point the witness to the numbered paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We also have an English version with the paragraphs numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that would be most helpful. That's extremely helpful. Thank you. That will enable us to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In fact, what I want you to do -- that was just a reference point. I want you to go, Mr. Gasi, please, to paragraph 21. It's a paragraph beginning: "When I got to Luka, a man with the surname Pudic." Do you have that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if you look through, about four or five lines from the -- please read through that paragraph, and then I'd -- before you do that, just draw your attention to a short sentence, which in English is: "I was not beaten."

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the translation of that remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I heard the translation to be "I wasn't beaten," but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It just didn't come through, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. "I was not beaten." Yes.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what your statement says. Yesterday in the evidence before this Tribunal, when you described what happened at Luka, you said: "A policeman from the Brcko police station took me there, and this guy whose name was Pudic was waiting for me there. He hit me with a pistol on the head and they took me into the first office on the right-hand side." So you seem to be -- it's some years later, but you seem to be unclear about whether Mr. Pudic did or didn't hit you, and back in 1995, much shorter after the events, you didn't suggest that he had hit you on your arrival. Is it that -- is that correct, that he didn't hit you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that he hit me, but in the statement -- I don't know why it's in the statement the way it is. Well, he did hit me on the side of the head. He didn't hit me actually on the head, but more on the side to my ear. I don't know why in the statement it says that he did not, but he did hit me on the right side of the head. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we look at page -- paragraph 26 in your statement, you refer to Mr. Pudic again. Do you see?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we go to look at your evidence yesterday, and this is at -- you don't have this, Mr. Gasi, but this is at page 89 of the transcript, for the reference. Mr. Hannis put to you: "You told us how the first day you arrived you were hit on the head by Mr. Pudic. Were you yourself personally physically abused during your 10 or 11 days at Luka besides that time?" And then you said, which is what you just said a moment ago: "He didn't hit me in the head. Actually, he missed my head and put me -- and hit me in the ear. But on that same day, I was beaten up. That was a bit later." Go back to your statement, please. If you look at the paragraph which is numbered 24 -- you see, it's a paragraph that begins: "At around 2.00 p.m." You say: "At around 2.00 p.m. I was beaten by Ivan, whose surname I don't know. After that incident I learnt from the other prisoners that his name was Ivan." And then you go on a few sentences later you say: "In his hand he held a wrench which is used to connect fire hoses." Do you see that reference?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had a wrench. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Ivan tried to hit me in the head but I moved my head. He hit the shoulder instead. He then hit me on the other shoulder and I fell on my hands and knees," and then you go on to describe that and then at the end of that paragraph you say, the last couple of lines: "I was bruised from the beating. I continue to have problems from the injury near my ear. The bones near my ear continued to ache for seven months after I was kicked."

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, I'm not putting it to you. Please don't misunderstand. I'm not putting it to you that you weren't at Luka or anything like that, but I do suggest to you that what you said in your statement in 1995, which was no mention of Mr. Pudic hitting you when you first arrived was correct and that after all this time you are tending to become confused about the different people involved here, that in fact it was Ivan who tried to hit you on the head but failed to hit you where he wanted to. It was not Pudic that hit you on the head at all. You're just perhaps not surprisingly getting some of these people mixed up.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you something. I was in Luka. For the two or three days that I've been here with the Prosecutor, I went through a lot, even more than from before the war. And I'm telling you now exactly the way it was. It could not have been any other way. Pudic did hit me with a pistol. In 2001, I went to meet this same Pudic in Brcko, but I couldn't find him. That was in the beginning, when they brought me to Luka. Did I tell this to The Hague investigators before, and perhaps they didn't put it in the statement? That I don't know. But I am telling you: Pudic did want to hit me on the head. I don't know. I dodged. And he did catch me on the right side of the head, and I was pushed into this office where he was. I described all of that. And also, you have the description of what happened with Ivan. You have it there, exactly as it happened, and it was the way it's described in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the position, you say, Mr. Gasi, is that in fact both Mr. Pudic and this other man Ivan tried to hit you on the head, both of them failed to hit you on the head in the way that they were attempting to do? Right so far?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he wanted, but he did want to hit me on the head. This was obvious. So he did hit me on a part of the head. Later, in the hangar, I described what happened between myself and Ivan. That's what happened. I don't know how to describe it in any other way. There's nothing else I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the reason that you didn't mention Mr. Pudic hitting you on your arrival in your statement that said that you were not beaten was you say that there must have been some omission in the writing down of what you said to the investigators in the statement?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you again: I don't know how it happened. I don't know whether I said that he hit me or not. I think that I did say it, and he did hit me, but I don't know why that's not included in the statement. I can't tell you that. But you can be sure yourself, and this Trial Chamber, that I am telling you only the truth. I'm telling you how it was and the way it was is the way it is described here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm just suggesting to you, Mr. Gasi, that there's every possibility that you get confused about these names and confused about these particular unpleasant incidents. You don't agree?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can be sure that I know very well who interfered with me in Luka from day one. You can be convinced of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. In your evidence yesterday, when you were talking about the events that you described as having witnessed on the 7th of May, that's the executions that you described to the Tribunal, you said that the policeman -- you were describing one of the incidents that you witnessed. You said: "The policeman who shot in their backs he wore a blue shirt with short sleeves of the kind the policemen used to wear before the war and also a pistol and the others who were all shooting at people they all wore, camouflage JNA uniforms with balaclavas, black balaclavas over their heads." Now, you remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. Perhaps I said yesterday that he wore a short-sleeved shirt. I remember that also. But if you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you said -- it's in the transcript. You said he wore a blue shirt with short sleeves. It's there on the record. If you look at -- this is in English, so I'm simply going to tell you what it says. But for everybody else's benefit, we have a transcript of evidence that you gave in a case. Do you recall giving evidence in a case against Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall, and I did give evidence in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
