utterances.text: And in that case, and this is at page -- it starts -- this particular transcript starts at page 6 of the clip of documents that we have. And I'll read it for your benefit as well, Mr. Gasi. It's at page 723 of that transcript, beginning -- I'll pick it up at line 19: "Yes, I was in the immediate --" well, I'll pick it up two lines above that. "So during this time between 30th of April and 27th of May when you were free for move about the town of Brcko, during that time, did you see any persons killed in the town of Brcko?" You said: "Yes, I was in the immediate vicinity when they shot civilians in the street." "When was that?" "On the 7th of May at 11.00 in the morning." "What did you see on that date?" And then you said: "In one part of town called Stari Grad, I saw civilians being shot in the middle of the street in groups of four to six to seven persons fired at, shot by men wearing camouflage uniforms of a grey-olive-green colour. And in the same place on the same spot they killed three men. They were killed by members of the civilian police in uniforms. That is, one of them shot three of them. He fired behind their backs at the back of their heads." The point I want to draw your attention to, Mr. Gasi, is you described the shooting as being done by men wearing camouflage uniforms of a grey olive-green colour. Then at page 726 of that same transcript, you are describing being taken from the police station to Luka. It's the same incident that you described in your evidence yesterday. You said at line 22, at page 726: "From the SUP," from the police station, "they took me to Luka. It is a site on the bank of the Sava, huge hangar. They took me there again in a civilian car belong to go an enterprise or something like that." And you were asked: "Who took you there?" And you said: "This time, they wore the uniforms of the reserve JNA, two of them. I know one of them. It was a local neighbour, a Serb from Brcko." So again, I'm drawing your attention to the fact you referred specifically, you said, "this time they wore the uniforms of the reserve JNA." And then at the -- on the same page, further down, you're being asked about the Luka camp. At line 16: "Q. While you were at the camp was the camp guarded?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What did these guards wear?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards were outside the hangars, around those hangars, and they again wore reserve JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there other camp personnel who were located inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were." What I'm drawing your attention to here, Mr. Gasi, is that you are very specific in your evidence in the case against Mr. Tadic, where you gave your evidence in 1996. You were very specific to make the point that on the second and third of those occasions that you're mentioning the men concerned were wearing JNA uniforms, whereas in relation to the shooting in the street which you had witnessed on the 7th of May, you did not mention JNA uniforms. Do you agree that that shows very clearly that you were intending to make that contrast and recognising that JNA uniforms had not been worn by the men involved in the first incident, the shooting in the street?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, and before 1992 as well, in the former Yugoslavia, nobody - please keep that in mind - nobody except the JNA had the right, nor were you able to freely buy anywhere in the territory of the former Yugoslavia any type of uniform. As far as I'm concerned, if you were issued a uniform, it was issued to you only from a JNA warehouse. There were changes in the federal army regarding the shades of the uniforms, and this was in the period from 19 -- to 1992. But from 1990 to 1992 you were able to see everywhere old reserve JNA uniforms, as well as uniforms of active soldiers of the JNA, as well as new camouflage uniforms which belonged to the JNA. The gentlemen who wore those uniforms, I don't know where they got them. I don't know whether they bought them or received them from the federal army. I was not able to buy a police uniform or such a uniform that they wore. Perhaps there were some places where you could buy such a uniform, but I didn't know them. That is all. I attempted, as much as I could, before the Trial Chamber, to describe all of this. That's how it was. I don't know that it happened in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the case against Mr. Tadic, you gave very similar evidence to the evidence you gave yesterday in relation to the arming of Serbs by the JNA, and you recall the evidence that you gave yesterday on that, that in your travelling around the area of Brcko in connection with your work, you did see people being armed?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that on several occasions, several times I saw things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You never mentioned, although you did say that in the Tadic case, I'm acknowledging that, you never mentioned that in the statement that you gave, the one that we looked at a little while ago, the written statement taken by the investigators. You didn't say anything at all about that, did you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they asked me, I must have answered. Whenever they asked me a question, I would tell them what I saw, that is, if I was asked what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it correct that at the time that we're talking about in early 1992, that weapons were only attainable from the JNA by becoming -- by joining the reservists of the JNA? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA reserve and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if the -- and the system that you describe of logging the issue of weapons, because you describe that and you would have to sign and there would be a little booklet I think is the way you put it, that's the system that applied in those circumstances, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the constitution of the former Yugoslavia was still in effect, and the Yugoslav People's Army observed the constitution. It's a fact. I didn't add anything to it, I didn't omit anything from it. What I saw is exactly what was being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I suggest to you is that you didn't see anything more than an entirely regular and legitimate issue of weapons.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday when the Prosecutor asked me about that, I told him that I had an opportunity to see lorries coming to Serbian villages and unloading boxes of rifles. There were civilians there waiting for the arms. They put a desk in front of the local commune building. They were handed out the weapons, and this was recorded in a log. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But isn't the position that you were just travelling around the area in the course of your work? Weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. I entered these buildings. I had to be there because my work took me there. And that's how I gained the opportunity to observe all that, and that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the point I'm making, Mr. Gasi, is you were there to do your work. Presumably you were getting on with your work. You weren't there to sit around and observe in detail what was happening in relation to weapons. So you actually don't know to whom the weapons are being issued, and you don't know that it wasn't simply a regular issue of weapons in the way that I've described.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen carefully, sir: I had plenty of time, and I even had a drink with those people. They even offered me a piece, because they thought that I was one of them, if that can help you to arrive at the truth. I had plenty of time to observe everything in great detail and to remember everything very, very well. So rest assured, I'm telling you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your evidence in the Milosevic case, and this is in the clip that we have, Mr. Milosevic cross-examined you relatively briefly, Mr. Gasi. He said that -- this is at 26446, Your Honours. And he asked you: "Who was fighting who in Brcko?" And your answer was: "To tell you the truth, I don't know."

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I will repeat it again. I don't know. I didn't see where shooting was taking place and who was there. That's what things were like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Stewart: In my copy, it jumps from 26444 to 26447.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour. I had -- I had thought that it was perhaps just my copy where that happened, and I knew what it said anyway. But, so, my apologies. Well, perhaps Your Honour can -- we'll take it from me it does say that and we will supply that copy to the Tribunal to make that gap good.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm missing the same pages, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. We'll fill in that for everybody if Your Honour will accept it on that basis, because I can assure Your Honour that that simple exchange is on the transcript, and I will provide that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you are literally quoting and in the context we have an opportunity to see that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. It's a very short exchange and I have a verbatim note of that. So that is exactly what the exchange was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The position in early 1992, and through into April, was, and I think this is the gist of what you've just been saying, Mr. Gasi, was, to put it mildly, extremely confused, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It may seem confusing to you, but to me it did not look confusing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, in circumstances where your answer to Mr. Milosevic on the question, well, who was fighting who, was that: "To tell you the truth, I don't know, Mr. Milosevic," I'd suggest that implies, since, according to you, there was a lot of fighting going on, that implies considerable confusion as to what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Here I think it would be very helpful to have the transcript, because I don't know if he's talking about who fighting who on a particular day, a particular part of town, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can help on that. Mr. Milosevic was -- it wouldn't take a couple of minutes to get it, but Mr. Milosevic, the full question, who was fighting who in Brcko, and he was talking about this time period, the same period about which this witness has given evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if it would be possible for you to provide us with the relevant transcript pages and return to this issue perhaps after the next break, or at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, except that I shall finish, I think, Your Honour, well before the next break. But I'm in Your Honour's hands. I'm delighted to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will see whether it's possible. I see Madam registrar already searching in the transcripts of the Milosevic case to see whether she can provide the pages so that we have a better idea of the context. If you could move to your next subject and we'll try to solve the and matter even before the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'll move to my next topic. In fact, yes, I -- all right. In the transcript of your evidence in this case - this is at pages 23, 24, and 25 - you gave evidence yesterday of a rally that you had attended. Do you recall that? And it was in fact a rally organised, you said, strictly speaking, it was organised by a cultural organisation in Brcko. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Serbian cultural and arts society, called Prosvjeta, enlightenment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And you said that everybody from the Serbian Democratic Party from Sarajevo appeared at this rally, except, you think, for Mr. Karadzic. And then in fact you asserted a bit more directly that he wasn't there. Is the position in fact that you're not sure whether Mr. Karadzic was there, or that you're saying your clear recollection is that he wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that rally, he wasn't there in that hall. The speakers introduced all of those who were present and those people whose names were called stood up. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And you said that you did see Mr. Krajisnik there. Again, is it that you think Mr. Krajisnik was there or that you are sure that he was there, in your own mind?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am absolutely positive that he was there with other SDS leaders, a hundred per cent. A hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik says he wasn't there, Mr. Gasi.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. We have no evidence of that at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that it's the position of the Defence that Mr. Krajisnik wasn't there? Because whether he says something, he has not told us, but that's, I take it, what is contained in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm surprised by the intervention because I would understand that's a perfectly conventional way of putting the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll get used to each other. That's how I understood it, and since Mr. Krajisnik, apart from his short statement, has not spoken a word, that's how I understood it so -- but we get used to each other's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sure we will, Your Honour. Rather than trying to adapt -- I will adapt my style, of course, as necessary but perhaps it's simpler if I just indicate that if I, at any point in this case, say "Mr. Krajisnik says" then it can be taken that those are our instructions on the Defence side and that when Mr. Krajisnik comes to give his evidence, that Mr. Krajisnik's instructions are that that's what he will say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do see that we have some different traditions, but if we try to understand each other's traditions, it will work out perfectly well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- I think, Mr. Gasi, you are not sure whether this particular cultural rally was before or after the referendum at the end of February 1992.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. Yesterday I said that it was after the referendum, but I can't be sure. I don't know whether it was before the referendum in Bosnia and Herzegovina or after it. I cannot recall that for a fact. But in any case, the rally was in the culture hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If you look at page 30 in the bundle of documents that we've given you today, you'll find a short note, and at page 29, Your Honour, is the English version. I couldn't say, in fact, which is the original. It probably is the English version. But I understand this is -- I'm informed by the Prosecution this is a note made by an investigator on behalf of the Prosecution. Have a look at that, Mr. Gasi. Would you just read perhaps the first bit down to the first line across the page. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is this the same rally?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was also a founding assembly of the SDS in Brcko in front of the cultural hall and Mr. Karadzic spoke. There was also a pre-election rally in 1990, and there was this rally in the culture hall when the cultural and arts society was being established. This was at the very end, when the Prosecutor asked me about this, and I spoke in general terms. I did not refer to any particular rally. If you want me to go in any detail, I'm willing to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm just asking you, first, whether -- we'll go into detail as necessary, but I'm asking you first, and I'm not a hundred per cent clear of your answer, whether you're saying that this is or possibly might be the same event as the one that you were just talking about a moment ago, at which you said Mr. Krajisnik was present.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where it says the SDS leaders would always make reference to the victimisation of Serbs in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Mr. Gasi. I haven't asked you to read on to the second paragraph. The first paragraph only was what I invited you to read, and it refers to an open rally. Mr. Karadzic visited Brcko. And I'm simply asking you whether it -- let's say, in your view, whether it definitely is, definitely isn't, or might be the same event as the one that we were talking about a moment ago, at which you said Mr. Krajisnik was present.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karadzic spoke at the founding assembly in front of the cultural hall. He was talking about red flags waving. And people who spoke in the cultural home at the next rally spoke along the same lines. They repeated Karadzic's words that he uttered at the founding assembly in front of the cultural hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You refer -- it's just that you refer specifically in your evidence yesterday to - and this is at page 24 of the transcript - you said: "There was also another gentleman from the Republic of Serbia who was introduced at the rally as the minister for the Serbs across the Drina River." Do you remember that? Do you remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's just that in this note that we're looking at, a similar point arises. Do you see towards the end of that first paragraph, it says: "There was also a minister from the government of Serbia present at the rally"? I'm just suggesting to you that maybe, given that reference, perhaps you'd like to rethink. Perhaps these are the same event.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, where Mr. Karadzic is mentioned, this was the founding assembly of the SDS. That's when he spoke about red flags. And then there was another rally in the culture hall, when his words were repeated by other people. And there were also a number of other local SDS meetings at which his words were repeated. I didn't omit or add anything. This is just a general view of the things. I can analyse each of these events if you want me to do that. I don't know what is disputable in all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, don't worry about that, Mr. Gasi. The -- when you gave your evidence yesterday about the cultural organisation meeting, you said, apart from Mr. Karadzic you said wasn't there, everybody else, including Mr. Krajisnik, Biljana Plavsic, Aleksa Buha, and Nikola Koljevic were there. When we look at this note of, according to you, it would be a different meeting, you say: "Almost all of the other SDS meetings in Brcko, a member of the republic SDS leadership would attend, like Koljevic, Plavsic, Aleksa Buha and others." So in fact you mention three of the four people you mentioned yesterday but not Mr. Krajisnik. Is there any reason why you don't mention Mr. Krajisnik or, put it more accurately, Mr. Krajisnik is not mentioned at all in this note?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was there in culture hall, and that's the truth. He was there, and that is a fact. I don't have any other answer to give you. The only person who was not in the culture hall at that time, during that rally, was Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a slightly different questions question, perhaps, Mr. Gasi. If we just concentrate on the note where you say: "At almost all of the other SDS meetings a member of the republic SDS leadership would attend, and then you name Mr. Koljevic, you name Mrs. Plavsic, you name Mr. Buha, you don't name Mr. Krajisnik. I'm really asking you why Mr. Krajisnik should be omitted from that list.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth be told, I really don't know why. But Mr. Krajisnik was in the culture hall on that occasion. I really don't know. I can't give you an answer. Mr. Krajisnik was there. And I subscribe to that. I am not going to say any differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that only leaves the point that was left over in relation to the page of the -- the missing page of Mr. Milosevic's transcript. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that Madam Registrar has distributed the failing pages. We have got them available. But before you go to the next -- to that issue, you introduced page 29 and page 30 as -- let me just look at it. If you look at page 30 in the bundle of documents, and on the cover page, we see "Document relating to Gasi" but it's totally unclear to me what kind of document this is. Is this a summary made by someone else or is it -- it's unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was unclear to me. Perhaps I mentioned it to quickly in passing a few minutes ago that it had been prepared by Mr. Wladimiroff. But I think Mr. Hannis has the exact details in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Stewart asked me about this before we started. In checking my file, the only information I had about this particular document is a form called "Information index form," which indicates that this was a statement of Mr. Gasi about several SDS rallies, that it was taken or noted down on the 1st of January, 1996, or at least it was submitted on that date; and the receiver of this information was Mr. Vladimir Tochilovsky, an attorney in our office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is not the same person as Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That must have been my mistake, Your Honour, because I wrote it down on a different piece of paper and I'd remembered it as Wladimiroff. One can see the connection, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That having been clarified, so it's a kind of an internal note prepared by the Office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not a signed document. I just want to know the status of that document. Yes. Then, Mr. Stewart, I think all the Judges now have pages 26445 and 26446 as well, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've acquainted ourselves with the context in which the question was put by Mr. Milosevic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just to remind ourselves and you, Mr. Gasi: You were being cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic, and he had asked you about those JNA airplanes that you had mentioned yesterday and bombing. I just want to ask you briefly, as it happens, about that. You said yesterday, and this was at page 53 of the transcript, that during the period up to your arrest on the 27th of May, you continued to work around Brcko. That's correct, isn't it? You did continue to move around Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the 10th of May to the 27th of May, I did move around Brcko and the suburban area of Brcko and that was all within the scope of the work that I had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we take it, then, since you never mentioned anything in your evidence, you certainly didn't see any evidence in your travels around Brcko of any bomb damage anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any bomb damage, if you're referring to the occasion when these two planes flew over and when I heard the explosions. I was in the vicinity, but I did not see any major damage. I saw damage on some of the houses, some glass was shattered. I don't know whether this was caused by the explosions that these two planes caused or maybe by the previous explosions when the two bridges had been blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Just returning, then, to the reference in the evidence when -- which I quoted to you, you were asked by Mr. Milosevic who was fighting who in Brcko and you said: "To tell you the truth, I don't know." And I suggested to you that it was a confused situation which you seemed reluctant to accept. You're still not prepared to accept that the situation in Brcko in April 1992 and before that was confused?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know who shot at whom. That's what I said. The question was confusing, so he must have received a confused answer. All I can tell you is that I don't know who did the shooting and who was shot at, and that's all I know, and that's the answer I gave him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You know, do you, that in the -- what are called the run-up to April 1992, there was not just a question of Muslims and Serbs, but there was also the question of incursions of army units from Croatia? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that, sir. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You don't know anything at all about that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. You can rest assured that I don't. And I can't tell you anything about that. I don't know anything about that, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know anything about an attack on a village of Sijekovac in February 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the taking over of the town of Odzak by members of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know anything about members of the 106th Brigade of the HVO, that's the Croatian Defence Council, it's translated as, who occupied Orasje? You don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, on the first example you gave, you indicated February 1992. The temporal context of the questions put by Mr. Milosevic are clearly early May 1992. Could you, for the other examples you just gave, also give a time indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In relation to Odzak, the time would be April, May, and June 1992. I'm not able to give a specific date in relation to what I said in relation to Orasje. And then -- well, apart from this, that I was coming on then -- I think I hadn't got there yet. April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the occupation by Croat and Muslim forces of municipalities of Bosanski Brod, Derventa, Modrica, Odzak, and Orasje? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. My only objection is in terms of relevance. I don't know how that pertains to Brcko or to the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it -- directly, Your Honour, because, after all, a lot of the thrust of this witness's evidence is that he knew what was going on. It's certainly relevant to explore the degree of knowledge or ignorance of this particular witness in relation to events in the whole vicinity in which the matters to which he gives evidence occurred. That's the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's not spend too much time on it. It has some relevance, because you're asking about the knowledge of the witness on events in approximately the same time period, and in view of his answer given in the Milosevic case, it has some relevance. But let's not spend too much time on it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- or invitation, because I have finished. In fact, I've finished my cross-examination altogether, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any need to -- first of all, I'd like to ask my -- first of all, I'd like to ask whether there's any need to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had about three questions I wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I had about three questions I wanted to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, could you explain to the Court what you mean by "reserve JNA uniforms" and the difference between JNA, TO, and police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reserve JNA uniforms were uniforms which were used up until 1992 in the JNA. I'm familiar with those. You were issued with a uniform to have one at home. But when you were called up, you had to have the same uniforms. That's what I know. The TO had similar uniforms in those colours. They were practically the same. And if you were called up to come to your enterprise, you had to come wearing a uniform, one of those uniforms. I don't know about any other uniforms. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, the second topic I wanted to discuss regarded your statement to the Helsinki Commission. Did you see a B/C/S translation of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have the opportunity to do so, and I wasn't asked to do so by those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you previously testify in the Milosevic case that you thought there was a bad interpretation of your statements to the commission?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was a misunderstanding in the interpretation, but those people were questioning me and I was telling them how it was. I wasn't adding any numbers or augmenting the numbers. What I saw, I told them. They also had interviews with other people who were coming to Denmark. There are refugees from Brcko in Denmark. I can't remember how long after that I received a letter with this alleged interview that I gave to them. I received it in the English language, and I couldn't make any corrections to that. I wish I could have done so, but I wasn't able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And finally, with regard to that note of interview concerning the rallies: Had you ever seen that note before? It was page 29 of the packet that Mr. Stewart showed you.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that here for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you had not signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, how could I have signed it if I hadn't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the statement indicated that you attended several SDS rallies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did attend several. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Stewart, is there anything that has arisen during cross-examination that would cause you to put further questions to the witness? And I perhaps clarify this: That if, in the answers during cross-examination, something new comes up, then this Chamber will usually allow you to put additional questions. Is there anything you'd --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's nothing at the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Sir, I would like to ask you to help me to confirm for me, so that I can see whether I understood your testimony properly. You stated that you had heard that you had seen a man who executed prisoners. I'm quoting what you said in English, or rather, that you heard the man say: "Thirty of them for one of mine." So you also said, as part of your testimony, that you can tell the difference in dialects, if I can put it like that, between Serbs and non-Serbs. So could you please tell me - this is my first question - that man, did he say that: "Thirty of them for one of mine"? And when he said that, did he speak in any particular accent, or did he speak in a particular dialect based on which you could conclude the ethnicity of that person?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not conclude what his ethnicity was. He was wearing a camouflage uniform. I couldn't conclude that based on the cap and his uniform. But he said: "Fuck their balija mothers, bre." So I don't know. But I think it's very likely that he was a Serb from Serbia, because they're the ones that use that word "bre." But I don't know. Perhaps he could have been also a Bosnian Serb using that word "bre."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what does "bre" mean?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what they use when they speak. It doesn't mean anything. They just add that at the end when they are speaking. Just like in Bosnia we say "ba" they use the word "bre." It doesn't mean anything. It's just something that is used. It's a colloquialism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for that answer. Now I would like to ask you another question. You said during your testimony, or rather, you mentioned the fact that some officers came to the Luka camp and that they wanted to find snipers there. When they found out that there were two professional snipers there, they treated those people well. So in your opinion, could you tell us why this was so. How do you explain, how do you explain that conduct towards somebody who happened to be snipers, who happened to be combatants, fighters?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not snipers. They used to take out those two people every day and beat them up. One of them, Jovo, his name is Muhamed but we called him Jovo, that man is still alive today. That man is retarded. That man couldn't even walk properly. He couldn't orient himself around town. And I don't understand why they called them, they nicknamed them, Muslim snipers. They used to beat him up every day. His left arm was broken. It was broken right here. He had injuries on his nose. The bone was sticking through there. And at that moment, he had fly spit on that wound. Maggots were coming out of that wound. They were beaten up every day. No one could go up to him and to that other man Blek in the prison just because they had this nickname attached to them: Muslim snipers. They just found them down there at Kolobara and brought them in. They had nothing to do with that. This JNA officer, this major who would come in with two police officers, and he said loudly to Kosta: "If these two are your Muslim snipers, fuck you. I wouldn't lose one single soldier here in Brcko. You should bring a doctor so that they could treat them, he could give them medical treatment, he could clean them up." That was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could you please explain why, why, how was it that they got this nickname? If you know. Please tell us, if you know.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I have no idea. As far as they were concerned I was a Muslim extremist myself. I cannot say, but they made me out to be a Muslim extremist, a fundamentalist. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now I would like to put my one-before-last question. It actually has to do with the first one. It's about what you heard when you heard that person who was executing people and who said that they would have to pay for each one of mine who had fallen, thirty of them for each one of mine. At that point, was there fighting underway already?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I heard shooting when I was in my apartment, as well as when I was at Elektro-Brcko. I heard loud shooting and I heard strong explosions. Across from that place where I was in the Elektrodistribucija, there were guns of the JNA, and they were firing. I don't know who fought whom and where the fighting was going on. When I was walking around the actual centre of town and I was walking also towards the Mujkici local community, there was no fighting but they were all there. The army was there. I saw two tanks near the medical centre. That's when we went to fix the electricity there. They weren't firing. I don't know who they were firing at. I don't know where this fighting was. I didn't see anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I understand you correctly, you were present when weapons were being distributed, and you believe that they were distributed to Serbs. On the other hand, the opponents, who did the other side receive weapons from? Who provided the weapons to the other side?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the other side, because I didn't see anything. Had I seen it, I would have told you about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now let's talk about the event when you were entrusted with throwing corpses into the river. Do you remember that? Were these inmates from the Luka camp or were these people who were killed in a different place?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. Mostly they were in a pile after we had passed the railway carriages, they were in a place that was flattened out, and there was gravel there. I don't know if those bodies were brought there or if they were killed in Luka. I just know that they were already there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said that they wore civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Did you ever have the opportunity to see -- well, actually, my question relates to the other side. Were they in uniforms or were they wearing civilian clothes, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the dead people that I saw over there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, not the dead people. But it was said that there was an exchange of fire. So in this exchange of fire, you said that there were paramilitary forces, there was the army, the JNA, or, namely, Serbs. But there was also the other side. We don't know who this other side was. According to what you know, did the people from the other side wear uniforms or not?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So do you, then, think that the bodies which you had to throw into the river, do you believe that these were people who were killed during this exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer to that question. I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My last question concerns your opinion. Since you explained to us in detail how you came to be released, could you please tell us: Do you believe that the guards who were at the camp were free to do as they wished, or was there -- or were they actually just carrying out orders, in a fashion? Were they allowed to bring anybody they wanted there and could they release anybody they wanted to, or was there some kind of authority, some kind of power who said: Well, this man should be freed, and this man should be detained?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. On one occasion when Kosta, this Kole, took me out to come to his office, after this interview, when he asked me about these names and when he gave me the names, and as I was leaving his office, at the door there was a piece of paper of A4 format. It was typed. That nobody was allowed to enter the camp. Nobody was allowed to enter the hangar without the supervision of the commander, Kosta, Kole, and that inmates were not permitted to be eliminated without his permission. And this was signed by the commander of the Luka camp, Kosta Simeunovic, Kole. Well, I don't know how the actual organisation worked. I cannot tell you that. I don't know that. But I was taken out. I was freed, upon the orders of Captain Dragan. That's how it was. I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this Captain Dragan, what was his function?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I met him that time in Zvornik, he was their commander - I guess, I don't know - of these Special Forces, these Red Berets. He was wearing a civilian uniform. Everybody referred to him as "boss."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. [In English] And thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question for you. You told us yesterday that you brought your wife and daughter to Bijeljina and that a friend had come from Belgrade. Did you accompany them to Belgrade or did you return to Brcko and left wife and your daughter in the hands of your friend?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I came back to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you did not accompany them to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gasi, this concludes your evidence, unless the questions of the Judges would raise any issue on which the parties would consider that they have to put additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: None for me, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just like to ask:

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Gasi, that "Nobody was allowed to enter the camp, nobody was allowed to enter the hangar, without the supervision of the commander, and that inmates were not permitted to be eliminated without his permission and this was signed by the commander of the Luka camp. Well, I don't know how the actual organisation works. I cannot tell you that." Mr. Gasi, it's unreal what you just said, isn't it, to suppose that you, as a detainee in this camp, had any knowledge at all of procedures such as what documents needed to be signed in order actually to authorise a detainee's release?

utterances.speaker: ISAK GASI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I answered to the question of the Judge. What was standing next to the door when I was leaving Kosta's office. But they came into the hangar with or without Kosta. They didn't kill anybody at the hangar when I was there but they did beat people up. I don't know as far as whether they were respecting orders or not, and I don't know what the mechanism was behind the scenes. I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This, Mr. Gasi, concludes your evidence in this Court. The Chamber would like to thank you for having come and for having answered questions of both parties and of the Bench. It's important for this Court to hear the evidence given by those who have been present at that time in the area. Thank you very much. You're excused. Mr. Usher, could you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as exhibits are concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as exhibits are concerned, first of all, the two Defence exhibits, it's not yet on the record what number they are. And, Madam Registrar, could you guide us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first Defence exhibit is the bundle of documents, 30 pages, will be exhibit D1, and the second exhibit, the English witness statement of Isak Gasi D2, and the B/C/S translation will be D2.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the Defence whether in D1, whether it would include the pages 26445 that would then - yes - that would then be page 2A in your numbering, and 26446 as page 2B, and then we continue page 3, the hand numbering on the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure that would be the most convenient way of doing it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D1, therefore, now counts two more pages than it initially had. I didn't hear any objections during the presentation of this evidence, so I take it that they can be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Same true for the Defence, I take it. Then all the exhibits we'll not mention them all again, but that's from P1, Madam Registrar, until P25, and D1 up until D2.1, admitted into evidence. Before we have a break, I've got -- we've got two minutes left. I'd like to make two short observations. First of all, as far as the efficiency of the examination is concerned. I wonder whether the question whether finally the coffee was brewed and drunk or not really had to take three minutes, whether we could not get better control in order to save time, and perhaps the same -- of course, the Chamber is not aware of the relevance of these details, but up until now, the relevance of these details have not become completely apparent to the Chamber. The same, for example, would be true for stopping at the gas station and stopping at the border. Unless, of course, there would be some specific issue in it. But the Chamber is not aware of that. That's one observation. The second observation is for the Defence. The Defence did not give Mr. Gasi much time to verify whether paragraphs 2 and 3 of his Copenhagen statement would be in line with the testimony he had given in the court. As a matter of fact, it was entirely unclear to me from the transcript of yesterday whether, and the witness clarified the matter, whether he brought his wife up to Belgrade, or only accompanied her to Bijeljina. A similar question mark could be put by the statement of Copenhagen, and therefore, I was a bit concerned that where the initial evidence was not clear in every -- on every issue, and if the same was true for the Copenhagen statement, that there is a risk that we get an answer that it's all confirmed where I saw at first already some possible, perhaps not very relevant, points where the statements and the testimony given yesterday were not fully concurrent and I'd like to urge the parties to be very cautious in that respect. We adjourn until 10 minutes to 5.00 -- to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me introduce to the Chamber Ms. Magda Karagiannakis, from the Office of the Prosecutor, who will be leading the evidence of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether I will be able to pronounce your name as smoothly as Mr. Harmon does, but I'll try to do my best, Ms. Karagiannakis. Yes. Your next witness, Ms. Karagiannakis, protective measures in place are?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: We informed -- as we previously informed Your Honour in our filing of the 22nd of January, this witness has previously testified, and the measures that were imposed in that case were the use of a pseudonym and image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And pursuant to 75(F) of the Rules, we understand that those are still in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, they're still in place. And we use the same pseudonym or do we use a different pseudonym? Oh, yes. We have -- the pseudonyms are the numbers, say to the KRAJ-224. Would that be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a little bit more difficult to pronounce than just a letter, but -- and facial distortion. That means that when the witness enters the courtroom, the blinds should be all down. Mr. Usher, would you please pull the blinds down. We'll wait until the witness is led into the courtroom. I take it that the first thing you'll do is to present the name sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the curtains can now be lifted again. We'd rather do that first. Witness, I'll just explain to you: Your face will not be visible, and we'll not mention your name. We'll call you "Witness 224" in the Krajisnik case. The screen will even not enable the persons in the public gallery to see your face, and it will not be visible on the television screens either. Before giving evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration, and I see that the text has already been handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Ms. Karagiannakis, counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Karagiannakis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Witness, you're going to be handed a piece of paper shortly. It's got your name on it. Please don't read out what's on the sheet of paper, but can you please confirm that this is indeed your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be Exhibit --?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P26, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm going to ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions, and in English, and they'll be translated into B/C/S, and that's what you'll hear coming through your earphones. And when you answer in B/C/S, I will then receive and the Court will receive an English translation. So I would ask you to take a break or a pause between my question to you and your answer back to me, and the Court, so that we don't have any unclarity on the transcript. Also, if at any time during the course of my examination you feel the need to take a break, please don't hesitate to say so. Now, what was your nationality before the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Where were you living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: In Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: With whom did you live before the war? Please don't mention any names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: With my family, with my husband.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did you have any children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Yes. I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: How old were they in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: 12 and 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And where were your children immediately before the outbreak of war in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Immediately before the war in Brcko, the school was out. My brother came to visit, and my brother took my children to Stirac [phoen]. We were reckoning we would join them and collect our children from there. This is what we used to do every year. My brother would take the children, the children would be down there during the summer, and then when we were given our annual leaves, we would go there for two or three weeks and then we would collect our children and take them back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis, in order to have -- to make the protective measures as effective as possible, it's sometimes preferable to ask questions of the background in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you have any further questions to that. Madam Registrar, could you please prepare a redaction for page 77, lines 4 up until 9. And if you have any further questions, we could turn into private session; if not, we'll continue in open session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I won't ask any further background questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, when did the war start in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Officially, I can't give you the exact date. The only indication I can give you is what it was like on the day when the bridges were blown up. I had to go to work. I was woken up by an explosion. I went to work. I was wondering what was going on. I didn't know that the bridge had been blown up. I tried to find out what had happened. I only heard this explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: When did you hear -- approximately what time did you hear this explosion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Early in the morning, before I was about to leave for work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did you hear later that day what had happened to the bridges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: When I arrived at work at 7.00, people were asking what had happened. They wanted to know what the explosion was. And then other workers who came from the direction of the town told us that it was either one or two bridges that had been blown up. I don't remember. I only know that there had been an explosion and that the bridge that was used for passenger traffic had been blown up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, what time did you arrive for work that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: A little before 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And what time was your shift due to finish that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did you notice anything unusual when you arrived for work that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: I noticed that a lot of people didn't turn up for work to take over the next shift. It was before the May holiday, and a lot of patients would normally be discharged over the holiday, because people wanted to spend their holidays with the family. So that was not unusual. However, it was unusual to see that half of the personnel did not turn up for work. For example, the person who was supposed to relieve me didn't show up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the people that didn't show up to work that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Most of them were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that the person that was meant to relieve you at the end of your shift didn't come. What did you do when they didn't arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: I felt duty-bound to stay. I couldn't leave my patients unattended. I felt obliged to stay on and to keep on working.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What time did the following shift end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: It was 7.00 on the following morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: This discomfort and tension grew, we felt isolated. There was a feeling of fear and discomfort. The doctors then decided for all of us to shift into the new wing of the hospital, on the ground floor, again to make things safer for the patients.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: At this point, could the witness please be shown premarked Exhibit 38.099, and could the registrar please assign an exhibit number to that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P27.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can you see that photo on your screen, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Yes. That is the entrance to the general hospital, the Brcko hospital. The building you can see in the back is the new wing. That is the building where we moved to. It was very hard for me at the beginning to recognise this building because the gate was freshly painted, the fence was freshly painted. There were no signs on the top of the building. The signs, if there were any, were in the Latinic script, so at first it took me a while to recognise this building. However, this is the gate that I used to go through every day when I came to work. However, I can confirm that this is the building of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can I ask you: You mentioned the signs were in Latin script. What sign do you see there on that picture? What script?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: This is now the Cyrillic script --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... In relation to this. I don't know that we need to, for the purposes of the witness's evidence, go into this sort of detail as to the gate to the hospital. I don't think that's the substance of her evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I'm simply seeking to establish the record as to exactly what the gate looked like, and the fact that this picture is different to it, so we can have absolute accuracy in the transcript. However, if Your Honours want me to move on, I can do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the gate of any specific importance at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: No. But what you can -- no. I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so. And may I also remind you that I just am about to sign another redaction. We have to take the protective measures very seriously. And if we enter into the building and exactly the part of the building, then of course, and if the distinction is made between certain categories of people working in that building, then finally it's not very effective any more. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did people come through that gate into the hospital building that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Civilians came from the surrounding houses. They were also scared. They were looking for a shelter. Our shelter was in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Do you remember how many civilians came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. They came from different directions, from Mujkici, from Raja. They entered from all directions. I didn't count them. And they entered through different gates. There was a room full of civilians at the end of the day. That's what I saw finally, a room full of civilians who had all come to seek shelter. There may have been some 40 or 50 people all together.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the witness's microphone -- the other microphone be switched on, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: There were men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please switch on the other microphone of the witness as well. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: You were describing the civilians in the basement. Can you please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime, there were two or three cases, as far as I can remember. I was called to tend to some civilians who had been shot at. There was a young man called Damir, who was around 20. His leg was bleeding heavily. He had to undergo an urgent surgery. His leg had to be amputated in order to save his life. There was another man, an elderly man, around 50, who was shot in the spine. He was in a coma. And he died within the space of one or two days. He succumbed to his wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Was that that first day when all the civilians came into the basement that you treated these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: People kept on coming. The hospital is rather big. I was in one place, so I couldn't see every single individual, but I did notice them coming. In the area where I was working, I could see people coming through the corridors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: You mentioned two people, Damir and Lutvo. Do you know what ethnicity Damir was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Damir was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: I knew it from his first and last names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Do you know how he came to be hurt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: He was in a street and he was shot by a sniper shooter. That's what he told us. And the bullet hit his largest artery, the femoral artery, in his leg.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: The second man, Lutvo, do you know what ethnicity -- what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: He was also a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Again, I knew his name. I knew his family. I knew him from before. He was the manager of a furniture store.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: How did he come to be hurt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: The nurse who took his data told me that he was still conscious. He was standing in front of his house door. He was going to lock his door --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I realise that hearsay is acceptable in this Tribunal, but this is in the nature of secondhand hearsay rather than firsthand hearsay. What she heard from the nurse that the man told the nurse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As you know, usually this Chamber and the Tribunal will pay proper attention to reliability in the evaluation of the evidence, rather than to stop witnesses to testify about it. The objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What did the civilians who were coming into the hospital tell you about what was going on in the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: They told us that the Serbian army had entered the town, that they spread all over the town, that they were looting, entering the bank, taking things from the house, all the valuables, whatever they could lay their hands on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. I didn't ask you -- I didn't let you finish your answer about what had happened to Lutvo. Can you please describe how he came to have his injuries.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Whenever a patient is admitted, his data is taken, his medical history. The nurse asked me to help her. She had a lot of patients. And she told me that he had been shot at in front of his house door. He was leaving the house. He was going to lock his door, and that's how he was hit in the lumbar part of his back. When I went to see him, he was in a coma. He was no longer conscious. And two days later, he died.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What happened the day after the civilians were coming into the -- came into the hospital? What happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: We heard information, we heard shots, we heard shelling. I worked in the middle of the building. I could hear shots and explosions. I didn't know what was going on. I just felt and heard shots. I guessed that there must have been fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did anybody else arrive at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: [In English] I want to ask if it's 3rd -- I get lost a little bit, 3rd or 4th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: The day after you treated Lutvo and Damir, did anybody come into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Can you help me and -- help me to remember whether it was on the 3rd or on the 4th of May? Can you help me and refresh my memory?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I'll just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis, could you please -- you see that on page 85, line 7, that the answer could not be understood. Could you please repeat your question that appears in page 85, line 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did anybody else arrive at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: The 4th of July -- on the 4th of July, in the afternoon, when the fighting -- we could hear that the fighting was coming closer and closer to the hospital. In the afternoon on the 4th of July, a group of six or seven soldiers came in. I recognised one of those soldiers. It was Dusko Tadic. He was our employee. He worked as a porter at the hospital. I did not recognise the other worker because he had a mask on his face. His face was painted. He had a black cap, so I didn't recognise him. I recognised Dusko Tadic by his voice. We had been working there for years. And the second name, when Dusko Tadic called this second person, when he called him on the walkie-talkie, I found out that his name was Bozo. And when Bozo replied, responded, I saw that Bozo spoke in a Serbian accent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the 4th of July. Are you certain that that is the month that the bridges were blown up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: 4th of July? Did I say the 4th of July? No. The 4th of May. I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: So soldiers came into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: How many soldiers came into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: About six or seven came through the main entrance, and they came in so quickly. I was waiting -- I was standing in the corridor. They just looked at me for a moment, and then they split up, going to one side and the other side, in order to check the wards, to check the floor. On the left side was Bozo and on the right side Dusko Tadic went to check that other side of the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can you describe what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Bozo was wearing a uniform, a camouflage uniform, with leaves. It was of olive colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What were the other soldiers wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: The same uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Were they carrying anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Yes. Weapons. They had automatic rifles. Each one of them had a radio. They were constantly communicating throughout the hospital. You could hear the sound of the walkie-talkies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Who appeared to be the leader?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: In my opinion - and it's only my opinion - since Dusko Tadic worked at the hospital, he knew every room, so he was the one who gave instructions, because he was talking to all of the soldiers all the time and you could hear the conversations: Where they should go, to what part of the premises. In that section where I was helping, where the people were who had been wounded from firearms, he just -- Bozo just came through that part quickly in order to check who was in the hospital, for their safety. So they just quickly looked through the corridors and went on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What happened after they searched the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: When they searched the hospital, they again met up in the corridor. They talked some more again amongst themselves, in the middle, where the elevators were. Then they went out. And then, after a little while, they began to bring in weapons. First they brought in some kind of cannon with a long barrel, which I saw for the first time. I just noticed that the barrel was very long. They also brought in some cases, some closed wooden cases. They brought that into the elevator and went up towards the roof.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Not a long time after that, you could hear explosions from the roof. The building was shaking and you could sense that there was firing from the top of the hospital. There was constant firing. You could sense the constant explosions. The walls kept shaking all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Did anybody else arrive after that at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Later, yes, another group of soldiers came in camouflage uniforms. They were led by a person who introduced himself as Mauzer, and he ordered his soldiers to go to all the wards, to order all the staff to assemble together and to go to the restaurant, the hospital cafeteria, where we spent our breaks and had our meals, that we should all assemble there, that that was the central place where a meeting was to be held.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Had you ever seen Mauzer -- the man who identified himself as Mauzer before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: So how did you know he was Mauzer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: He introduced himself. He introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: You said that you were asked -- ordered to go to the cafeteria. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: He ordered us to line up from the door. It was the men first; the doctors, then the rest of the medical staff. There were some technicians. And then finally a few women doctors and some female nurses. So we stood there in a semicircle and he stood in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: When you say "he," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: I'm thinking of Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Do you know what ethnicity Mauzer was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Yes. He said his name was Mauzer and that he is from Bijeljina. He even said that he was a social worker. And he said that he -- that this was the territory that he is occupying, that he is responsible for that, and that nothing should be done without his knowledge; and if anything was done without his knowledge, that he would execute us. That was a kind of meeting. He issued us instructions that we should be very careful what we were doing, that we were under his control, and that we should not do anything without his control, anything that he didn't like. I don't know what he meant. And that we would be punished if that were to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What did Mauzer do, if anything, after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Yes. Then he started questioning people, and then it just happened that there was Dr. Popovic there. He's a man from Belgrade. He's a well-known surgeon. Everybody respected him. He asked him what his name was. He said his name was Petar Popovic, Cedomir. Then he started to get angry: How come that he was there amongst us? Why didn't he leave? Why did he stay to work with the Muslims and the Croats? Something to that effect. He said: "You've betrayed us. You don't want to belong to your own people." Then he slapped him sharply on his cheeks, in such an ugly way that he was -- he broke out in a sweat. His cheeks swelled up. He just didn't know what to make of all of that. He was confused. He was lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What ethnicity was Popovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: He was born in Serbia, from Belgrade, and he spoke in the Ekavian dialect. We all knew that. Nobody was bothered by that. He was a very good person. I also respected him as a nurse. He was of Serbian ethnicity, but nobody minded that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: After that, he went down the line, questioning the next doctor: What was his name. And then he also slapped more people. He was angry. He wanted to show his strength. And this fear -- he wanted to show how strong he was, and he went from one person to another and slapped those people. These were -- this was not a punch, like in a boxing match, but they were powerful slaps, so that each person's cheeks swelled up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of the people that were slapped? Please, don't mention the names. Just tell me if you do remember them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What were the ethnicity of the people that were slapped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: There was one Croat, and the rest were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: After that, he said that we had to be very careful about what we did. He did not want to repeat his instructions again. And now we could go back to work. So we went back to work to carry on as we were before they came.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: After you went back to work, were you given any other instructions by any other person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Yes. I forgot that. He said: Since the glass was shattered from the explosions, he said that the hospital had to be cleaned, completely cleaned, and he charged the staff to go through the wards, to clean up the glass, and to prepare everything, because some vojvoda, an important person was coming and the hospital had to be cleaned and ready to welcome him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: When you say "vojvoda," what do you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
