utterances.text: It's a high rank. I don't know myself. Vojvoda. It's a high rank. There were colonels in the Yugoslav People's Army. Vojvoda was a term that was used before the war, for people who belonged to the Chetnik groups, before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- tell the Judges what happened that evening.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Yes. We went back to our workplaces. We started to clean the glass. We distributed -- we went to all the different wards. We split them up amongst ourselves. We didn't even finish everything when a soldier came, and he asked for me. He said: "Who is this person?" I said: "It's me." He said: "Madam, will you come with me." So I went with him. I was just walking a little bit behind him so that I would know where we were going. He was actually taking us directly to the basement, where I saw, in the corridor in front of the sterilisation room, three other persons who were also waiting there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Without mentioning their names, can you tell us whether you knew those other persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Yes. They were hospital employees.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge -- first of all, were you in any way involved in any military activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: All of my life, I considered myself to be a medical worker. I didn't understand much about politics. I wasn't interested in politics then. I'm not interested in it now. I was a family person. I went to my work. My whole life was split between my work and my family. So I did not have any political leanings or tendencies, and I did not have any religious leanings. I understand that I was of the Muslim faith, but I never minded who was of what faith. I respected each patient who came to me. For me, they were all the same. I viewed all the people in the same way. I did that before, and I do that still today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: The other three people that you met with in the basement, do you know whether any of them were involved in any military activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: As far as I know, I don't know. I don't know whether they were or not. I know that they used to come to work regularly. They used to do their work. I know that. After work hours, I don't know what anybody else did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, this soldier who took you to the basement, what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: It was also a uniform with -- the soldiers who were standing around guarding those three persons also wore olive uniforms covered with leaves, as if it was camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, after you were all together, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: They just told us to go with them. They lined us up. One of them was in front, one of them was at the back, and they took us outside to a van, to some kind of vehicle. I don't know what kind. And we just sat in the back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: In the back, when we sat down inside, there were four soldiers there already, dressed in black. They had a lot of weapons on them. They were shaved on the sides and at the top they had long hair. They looked strange. The uniform they had was completely black. They were sitting together with us in the back. There was the driver. And we set off. There was no conversation at all until they brought us to the place that they meant to bring us to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What was the place that they meant to bring you to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: They brought us inside through a gate, to the Luka, which I knew of as a warehouse, although I had never been inside before the war. I didn't know what it looked like. I just knew that it was a place, that it was some kind of warehouse, and that it was called Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, in between the hospital and arriving at Luka, what route did you take?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Yes. We took the regular road through the town. I looked outside the window. I looked through the window, because we had all -- we were all speechless. In a way, we were frozen. We went through that -- all that was happening in that way. We were beginning to feel fear. We were shaking. Nobody was saying anything. We just looked through the window as we were passing through the town. It was an even greater shock to see the destruction in the town, glass everywhere. Four or five people were lying on the ground. Not in a group, but as we were driving past, you would see one body lying on the sidewalks as we were driving by. They were just lying there. Then we were gripped by an even greater fear. So not one word was uttered in that van, until we got to Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Were you able to see what the -- how the bodies on the ground were clothed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: Yes. They were civilians. They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: How do you know they were civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: You could see the jeans, sweaters, T-shirt, trainers, shoes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Now, you say you arrived at Luka. What was the date of your arrival at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: The 4th of May. It was already twilight. Night was falling.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: If at this stage the witness can be shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just intervene and ask one short question to the witness. You said that you saw four or five people lying on the ground. Were these people alive or were they dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not moving. They lay still. As the car was driving past and as we looked, that person did not move. The persons remained in the same position still, as if they were asleep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown premarked Exhibit 38.071. If that can be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P28.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: If you can, can you tell us what that picture shows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: It's Luka, Luka, where we were brought.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And can the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 15, which is premarked Exhibit 38.083.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P29.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I think that photo was shown to the previous witness and was marked with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: -- The number P15.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: If you can, can you tell us what that picture shows.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: It depicts Luka and the gate, as well as the office building on the right side. Just one moment, please. On the left side was the hangar, and on the right side were the offices. As you come in through the entrance, on the right side were the offices, and the hangar was on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: What happened to you when you arrived at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-224
utterances.text: They told us -- they brought us into a room, these four soldiers. They went off somewhere. There was a police officer inside, in a light-blue shirt and darker trousers. I know from before that this is a police uniform. The man got up. He stood up from the chair and he was there inside. He was very kind. He asked us to sit down. He offered us something to drink, and he just told us: "Please don't be afraid. This is just a formal questioning. Relax. You have no reason to be worried." He was really kind and he was trying to convince us that this was just a mere formality, that it was just a formality for questioning. He brought some people coffee and juice, whatever we wanted. He made sure we had something to drink. But the person who was -- until the person who was supposed to do the interrogating came, he wanted us to just take a little rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can I stop you there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: And can the witness please be shown premarked 49.61A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis, would you please keep in mind that we have to stop in a couple of minutes. So if you find a suitable moment -- I don't know how many questions you have on this exhibit, but would you please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can break now, because there are a series of questions that flow from this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise. I had to deal with some technical questions. Witness 224, it's close to 7.00. We'll stop and we'll continue tomorrow, in the afternoon, at a quarter past 2.00. The usher will escort you out of the courtroom, and then we expect you to come back tomorrow. But may I instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given, or on issues you might be asked about tomorrow. And please, Mr. Usher, would you escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just wait for one second until the curtains are down. Would one side be enough? The witness will -- no. No. We have to wait. Meanwhile, I'd like to make a very few observations. Ms. Karagiannakis, sometimes the evidence is a bit repetitious compared to what we've heard already. For example, showing the P15, which by mistake I think is announced as P29, but that's the photo already shown, did not appear to be a very contentious issue that this is the camp and where the hangars are. So therefore, it still takes almost two minutes to get that, and I don't know whether an aerial picture adds very much, unless, of course, at a later stage you have some specific questions in relation to that. Similarly, you asked twice how many soldiers came into the hospital. You asked, where the witness already said that Mauzer introduced himself under this name, you asked then -- could we try to be just as efficient as possible, leave out details. For example, I don't know whether all the details of the arrest and the place where the witness worked were of that importance, I think, for the Chamber, but of course unless it will turn out to be otherwise. Most important is that she was arrested by what kind of people and where she was brought. It's not up to the Chamber to say what details are of importance or are not of importance, but for that reason the Chamber urges the parties to keep that clearly in mind. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 6th day of February 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.
